# SOURCE_DOCUMENT: animators_survival_kit.json
# SOURCE_SHA256: 0ee95c2c9c48f3fd3d3652b1ddfbb86ff0e06695514b14b87257e3ddd2249fb2
# EXTRACTION_PROVIDER: local-json
# STATUS: VERIFIED
# AUTHORITY: OFFICIAL_DOCUMENT

{
  "handbook_metadata": {
    "title": "The Animator's Survival Kit",
    "subtitle": "A Manual of Methods, Principles and Formulas for Classical, Computer, Games, Stop Motion and Internet Animators",
    "author": "Richard Williams",
    "author_title": "Director of Animation 'Who Framed Roger Rabbit'",
    "historical_scope": "Traces the evolution of movement from ancient cave paintings (35,000 years ago) and 19th-century optical toys (Zoetrope, Praxinoscope) to the Golden Age of Hollywood animation (1930s-1950s) and modern 3D CGI / digital pipelines.",
    "core_purpose": "To distill decades of accumulated studio secrets, timing formulas, and performance mechanics from legendary master animators into a systematic, practical working order."
  },
  "topics": [
    {
      "topic_id": "topic_01",
      "title": "Foundations of Animation",
      "chapters": [
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_01",
          "title": "Why This Book",
          "summary": "Richard Williams explains his rationale for writing the handbook: to bridge the gap between crude formula drawing and true performance mastery. He outlines his personal journey seeking out master animators across studios (Warner Bros., Disney, Fleischer) to learn the 'invisible magic' ingredients of movement, weight, and character vitality.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Animation as Performance in Time",
              "content": "Animation is the art of performance in time, not static design."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Foundational Mechanics",
              "content": "Mastery requires acquiring the foundational mechanics developed during Disney's Golden Age (1930-1940)."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "Computer Animation as Puppetry",
              "content": "Computer animation is an extension of puppetry (high-tech marionettes) and relies on the exact same principles of weight, timing, and empathy as classical hand-drawn animation."
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_02",
          "title": "Drawing in Time",
          "summary": "Traces the historical human urge to depict movement across time, from 35,000-year-old Paleolithic cave paintings of multi-legged boars to 19th-century mechanical devices and early cinema pioneers.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "35,000 BP Cave Paintings",
              "content": "Cave paintings depicting animals with extra legs to show motion."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "1867 Zoetrope",
              "content": "Zoetrope ('Wheel of Life') invented in the USA."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "1877 Praxinoscope",
              "content": "Emile Reynaud invents the Praxinoscope using 30-foot strips of transparent 'Crystaloid'."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_04",
              "title": "1868 Flipper Book",
              "content": "The Flipper Book appears worldwide as the simplest device for drawings in time."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_05",
              "title": "1908 Fantasmagorie",
              "content": "Emile Cohl creates 'Fantasmagorie' in Paris line drawings on black background."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_06",
              "title": "1911 Winsor McCay",
              "content": "Winsor McCay animates 4,000 drawings for 'Little Nemo', followed by 'How a Mosquito Operates'."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_07",
              "title": "1914 Gertie the Dinosaur",
              "content": "Winsor McCay performs live with 'Gertie the Dinosaur', creating the first personality animation."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_08",
              "title": "1930s Disney Principles",
              "content": "Disney studio formalizes principles of weight, squashing, stretching, and character articulation."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_09",
              "title": "Level 1: Drawings That Walk",
              "content": "Drawings that walk (captivating basic motion)."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_10",
              "title": "Level 2: Drawings That Walk and Talk",
              "content": "Drawings that walk and talk (adding speech and synchronisms)."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_11",
              "title": "Level 3: Drawings That Walk, Talk, and Think",
              "content": "Drawings that walk, talk, and THINK (creating the illusion of an internal thought process)."
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_03",
          "title": "Time to Draw",
          "summary": "Emphasizes life drawing as the ultimate antidote to formulaic, stale cartooning. Williams argues that animators must understand underlying skeletal/muscular structure and real-world mass in order to caricature or exaggerate convincingly.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Formulaic Drawing",
              "content": "Robert Graves' Epitaph: 'He found a formula for drawing comic rabbits... so in the end he could not change the tragic habits this formula made.'"
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Perspective and Life Drawing",
              "content": "Winsor McCay's rule: Learn perspective and solid life drawing first before attempting animation."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "Knowing the Figure",
              "content": "Milt Kahl's rule: 'You have to know the figure well enough so that you can concentrate on the particular person - on the difference.'"
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_04",
              "title": "Drawing and Acting",
              "content": "Art Babbitt's rule: 'If you can't draw - forget it. You're an actor without arms and legs.'"
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "topic_id": "topic_02",
      "title": "Timing, Spacing, and Movement",
      "chapters": [
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_04",
          "title": "It's All in the Timing and the Spacing",
          "summary": "Explores the fundamental mechanics governing animation: Timing is the amount of time (number of frames) an action takes; Spacing is the distance a drawing moves between frames. Manipulating spacing changes velocity, acceleration, weight, and emotion.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Timing",
              "definition": "The number of frames allotted for an action to occur (e.g., 12 frames = 1/2 second)."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Spacing",
              "definition": "The physical gap or distance between consecutive drawings on a path of action."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "Coin Experiment",
              "content": "Two coins sliding across a table: Even spacing produces uniform, weightless speed. Progressive spacing (close together then farther apart) creates acceleration and mass."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_04",
              "title": "Bouncing Ball Experiment",
              "content": "Clustered drawings at the apex (slow in / slow out) create gravity-defying height, while wide spacing near the ground conveys impact and velocity."
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_05",
          "title": "Lesson 1",
          "summary": "Walks through the simplest practical exercise in spacing and timing: animating a bouncing ball to master squashing, stretching, gravity acceleration, and arc flow.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Apex and Impact Positions",
              "steps": [
                "Establish top apexes and bottom impact contact positions."
              ]
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Progressive Gravity Spacing",
              "steps": [
                "Apply progressive spacing increasing as the ball falls under gravity."
              ]
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "Squash and Stretch",
              "steps": [
                "Apply squash at impact (maintaining mass volume) and stretch on immediate recoil frames."
              ]
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_07",
          "title": "More on Spacing",
          "summary": "Examines advanced spacing techniques to prevent stiff or mechanical inbetweens, focusing on arcs, movement within mass, and the elongated inbetween.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Watch Your Arcs",
              "content": "Natural living motion moves in curved arcs, not straight lines. Bouncing balls, arm swings, and head turns must follow smooth parabolic or circular arcs."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Head Turn Rule",
              "content": "When a character turns their head from left to right, dip the head down or lift it up on the middle breakdown to prevent a flat, dead rotation."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "The Elongated Inbetween",
              "content": "Stretching/distending an inbetween drawing on fast actions (zip turns, door pounding) to create a motion-blur illusion without strobing."
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "topic_id": "topic_03",
      "title": "Animation Workflow and Production",
      "chapters": [
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_06",
          "title": "Advancing Backwards to 1940",
          "summary": "Deconstructs the golden-era production workflow used by major Hollywood studios, explaining the evolution of charts, keys, breakdowns, exposure sheets, and peg systems.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Keys",
              "content": "Storytelling drawings that define what happens in the shot. Circled on drawings."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Extremes",
              "content": "The outer limits of an action (highest/lowest/farthest points). Not circled on drawings."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "Breakdowns",
              "content": "The middle passing drawing that connects two extremes and dictates the arc/path of action."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_04",
              "title": "Inbetweens",
              "content": "Subordinate drawings placed between extremes and breakdowns to smooth out motion."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_05",
              "title": "Straight Ahead Animation",
              "content": "Animating drawing by drawing sequentially (1, 2, 3, 4...). Excellent for wild, spontaneous flow, fluid, fire, and drapery; dangerous for structure and timing budgets."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_06",
              "title": "Pose-to-Pose Animation",
              "content": "Planning storytelling keys and extremes first, then filling in breakdowns and inbetweens. Excellent for clarity, structure, and budget control; risks looking cold or mechanical."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_07",
              "title": "Combination Method",
              "content": "The master method. Plan storytelling keys and major extremes first, then perform straight-ahead passes on secondary parts (head, arms, clothes, hair, tail) over top."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_08",
              "title": "Exposure Sheet / X-Sheet",
              "content": "A 6-column grid where each horizontal line represents 1 frame of film (24 frames = 1 second; 16 frames = 1 foot).",
              "columns": [
                "Action",
                "Dial (Dialogue)",
                "Cel Level 1 (Main)",
                "Cel Level 2",
                "Cel Level 3",
                "Cel Level 4/5",
                "Camera Instructions"
              ]
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_09",
              "title": "Ken Harris Numbering System",
              "content": "Number drawings on twos sequentially (1, 3, 5, 7, 9...). Add 'A' drawings (e.g. 3A) when inserting ones for fast actions."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_10",
              "title": "Milt Kahl Numbering System",
              "content": "Use camera dial numbers directly on odd numbers for twos (1, 3, 5, 7...). Even numbers (2, 4, 6...) automatically signify ones without letters."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_11",
              "title": "Top Pegs vs Bottom Pegs",
              "content": "Warner animators (Ken Harris) preferred top pegs (flipping drawings); Disney animators (Frank Thomas) preferred bottom pegs (rolling drawings)."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_12",
              "title": "Perspex Disc",
              "content": "Roy Naisbitt's innovation of taping peg bars onto a Perspex disc for mobile panning."
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "topic_id": "topic_04",
      "title": "Character Locomotion",
      "chapters": [
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_08",
          "title": "Walks",
          "summary": "The master class on walk mechanics. Williams breaks down human locomotion as 'falling forward and catching yourself', detailing positions, timing charts, weight shift, and personality variations.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Fundamental Concept",
              "content": "A walk consists of 4 core positions per step: Contact, Down (Recoil), Passing Position (Breakdown), and Up (Push-Off)."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Contact Position",
              "content": "Both feet touch the ground. Front heel contacts; back toe pushes. Head is at a medium height. No weight on front foot yet."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "Down / Recoil",
              "content": "The lowest point in the walk. Front leg bends to absorb body weight. Knee is flexed; pelvis drops. Weight is fully felt."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_04",
              "title": "Passing Position",
              "content": "The lifted back leg swings past the supporting straight leg. Head rises back to medium height."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_05",
              "title": "Up / Push-Off",
              "content": "The highest point in the walk. Supporting leg extends fully onto ball of foot, pushing the body forward before the next contact."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_06",
              "title": "Walk Timing Reference",
              "timings": {
                "4_frames": "Very fast run (6 steps/sec)",
                "6_frames": "Run or very fast walk (4 steps/sec)",
                "8_frames": "Slow run or cartoon walk / fast stride (3 steps/sec)",
                "12_frames": "Brisk, natural business walk / March time (2 steps/sec; 1/2 sec per step)",
                "16_frames": "Leisurely stroll (2/3 sec per step)",
                "20_frames": "Tired, elderly, or heavy person (almost 1 sec per step)",
                "24_frames": "Slow, deliberate step (1 sec per step)",
                "32_frames": "Exhausted / 'Show me the way to go home' walk"
              }
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_07",
              "title": "Contact Method - Milt Kahl",
              "content": "Plot both Contact drawings first, then insert Passing Position, then Down and Up. Best for natural, grounded walks."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_08",
              "title": "Down Position Method - Art Babbitt",
              "content": "Plot the 2 Down positions first, then insert Passing Position and Up. Best for eccentric, invented, or comedic walks."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_09",
              "title": "The 15 Vitality Rules",
              "rules": [
                "1. Lean the body (forward for speed, backward for hesitation).",
                "2. Use straight legs on contacts and push-offs.",
                "3. Twist the body - tilt shoulders and hips opposing each other.",
                "4. Flop the knee in or out on passing positions.",
                "5. Tilt the belt line favoring the leg that's lowest.",
                "6. Flop the feet - delay foot leaving the ground.",
                "7. Delay toe leaving the ground until the very last instant.",
                "8. Tip the head or make it go back and forth.",
                "9. Delay parts - don't have everything working together at the same time.",
                "10. Use counteraction - fat, buttocks, breasts, clothing, pant legs, hair, tail.",
                "11. Break the joints - bend elbows and wrists against motion.",
                "12. Add more ups and downs for heavy weight.",
                "13. Use different timings on legs vs. arms vs. head.",
                "14. Twist the feet - take them off parallel alignment.",
                "15. Alter one tiny part of a normal walk to invent something brand new."
              ]
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_10",
              "title": "Sneak Types",
              "types": {
                "slow_sneak_ken_harris": "32-frame step (1.5 feet). Arms balance, head back, foot placed down gingerly with even spacing.",
                "bill_tytla_duck_sneak": "36-frame step on 4 planning drawings. Shape changes from curve to opposite curve.",
                "tip_toe_sneak": "Fast piston-like leg action on ones (4, 5, or 6-frame steps) with body crouched low."
              }
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_09",
          "title": "Runs, Jumps and Skips",
          "summary": "Examines locomotion at higher speeds. The fundamental difference between a walk and a run is that in a run, BOTH FEET leave the ground during airborne flight frames.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Walk vs Run",
              "content": "In a walk, one foot is always on the ground. In a run, there is at least 1, 2, or 3 frames where both feet are completely off the ground (airborne flight)."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Head-Up Rule",
              "content": "When raising the body on the Up position of a run, raise it only 1/2 head or 1/3 head. Raising a full head height creates unnatural bouncing."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "6-Drawing Run",
              "content": "Standard realistic run (4 steps/sec). Features Contact, Down, Push-off, Passing, Up (Airborne), and Landing."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_04",
              "title": "4-Drawing Run",
              "content": "Fast short-legged run (6 steps/sec). Arms stretched out in front; legs work under and behind."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_05",
              "title": "3-Drawing Run",
              "content": "8 steps per second (Tex Avery cartoon speed). Uses minimum 3 leg positions to create circular rotation without flickering."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_06",
              "title": "2-Drawing Run",
              "content": "Ultra-fast cartoon run (12 steps/sec). Alternates two extreme positions to defy gravity."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_07",
              "title": "Jump Mechanics",
              "content": "Consists of Anticipation (Crouch/Squash), Push-Off (Extension), Airborne Flight (Arc), Landing Contact (Impact/Squash), and Recovery."
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "topic_id": "topic_05",
      "title": "Weight, Flexibility, and Force",
      "chapters": [
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_10",
          "title": "Flexibility",
          "summary": "Details methods for avoiding rigid, stiff 'wooden' animation through joint breaking, overlapping action, drag, and counteraction.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Breaking Joints",
              "content": "Bending elbows, wrists, and knees in the opposite direction of movement during transit to simulate fluid, supple joint articulation."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Overlapping Action",
              "content": "When the main body stops or changes direction, secondary appendages (hair, ears, tail, clothes, fat) continue moving and catch up later."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "Counteraction",
              "content": "When one part of the body moves in one direction, another part moves in the opposite direction (e.g. when body goes up, stomach/breasts/drapery go down)."
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_11",
          "title": "Weight",
          "summary": "Focuses on convincing mass and gravity representation. Weight is not shown by smooth level motion, but through the ups and downs of body masses.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Weight and the Down Position",
              "content": "We feel weight on the DOWN position where legs bend and body mass drops under gravity."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Effort and Pressure",
              "content": "To show a character pushing or lifting a heavy object, exaggerate the force applied against the ground and show resistance in body muscles."
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "topic_id": "topic_06",
      "title": "Anticipation and Accent",
      "chapters": [
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_12",
          "title": "Anticipation",
          "summary": "The anatomical and dramatic law that every action must be preceded by a reverse preparation movement (e.g., bending knees before jumping, pulling hand back before throwing).",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Core Rule",
              "content": "Anticipation prepares the audience's eyes for what is about to happen so they don't miss the main action."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Anatomical Anticipation",
              "content": "Physical necessity (crouching before jumping)."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "Dramatic Anticipation",
              "content": "Directing audience attention (looking down at a box before opening it)."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_04",
              "title": "Invisible Anticipation",
              "content": "A 1-frame micro-crouch or reverse movement that adds snap without being explicitly seen."
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_13",
          "title": "Takes and Accents",
          "summary": "Covers cartoon takes, surprise reactions, and rhythmic accents.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Hard Accent",
              "content": "An abrupt, sharp movement or impact that bounces back upon landing."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Soft Accent",
              "content": "A cushioned, fluid accent that continues through into an extension or overlap."
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "topic_id": "topic_07",
      "title": "Advanced Animation Mechanics",
      "chapters": [
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_14",
          "title": "Timing Staggers, Wave and Whip",
          "summary": "Explores complex fluid and vibrational dynamics.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Stagger Timing",
              "content": "F秩序ing an action back and forth rapidly between two drawings (e.g., 1-3-2-4-3-5) to create trembling, shivering, or heavy strain."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Whip and Wave Action",
              "content": "Passing energy down a flexible jointed structure (whip, tail, ribbon) where each segment lags behind the preceding segment."
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "topic_id": "topic_08",
      "title": "Dialogue and Acting",
      "chapters": [
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_15",
          "title": "Dialogue",
          "summary": "Rules for synchronizing lip movement and speech accents with audio tracks.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Sound Sync Rule",
              "content": "Hit major mouth shapes and accents 1 or 2 frames BEFORE the sound is heard on the track. If synced exactly on the frame, speech feels late to the eye."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Phrasing",
              "content": "Group speech into rhythmic phrases and body attitudes rather than flapping the jaw on every individual syllable."
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "chapter_16",
          "title": "Acting",
          "summary": "The highest level of animation mastery: making drawings appear to think, feel, and make choices.",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Change of Expression",
              "content": "Execute expression changes during a head turn, tilt, or eye blink rather than holding static."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Contrast",
              "content": "Juxtapose broad action with quiet stillness; quiet moments make big accents explosive."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "The Acting Point",
              "content": "Identify the single main emotional or dramatic point of each shot and build all secondary action to support it."
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "topic_id": "topic_09",
      "title": "Master Animator Principles",
      "chapters": [
        {
          "chapter_id": "mentor_01",
          "title": "Ken Harris",
          "studio_affiliation": "Warner Bros. (lead animator for Chuck Jones)",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 1",
              "content": "Hey Dick, you're starting to draw those things in the right place."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 2",
              "content": "Draw that one first. That's an important drawing. (On storytelling keys)"
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 3",
              "content": "Look, you don't call me Mister Ken. Put the letter behind so all you think of is the numbers. (On numbering drawings B-1 as 1-B)"
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_04",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 4",
              "content": "I draw anything which is not a simple inbetween. (On workload division)"
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_05",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 5",
              "content": "I've done hundreds of walks, but I still want to get a test of my basic thing before I start to build on it."
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "mentor_02",
          "title": "Milt Kahl",
          "studio_affiliation": "Disney ('Nine Old Men' master draftsman)",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 1",
              "content": "I don't think it's possible to be a top notch animator without being an excellent draftsman."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 2",
              "content": "In a walk, or anything, I make the contact positions first - where the feet contact the ground with no weight on them yet. It's kind of a middle position for the head and body parts... It's a dynamic, moving thing."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 3",
              "content": "Whenever I see my drawings with odd numbers on them, I know I'm on twos and when I see even numbers, I know I'm on ones."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_04",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 4",
              "content": "I do a lot. I think about it a lot, and I do a lot."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_05",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 5",
              "content": "I do enough to have iron clad control over the scene."
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "mentor_03",
          "title": "Art Babbitt",
          "studio_affiliation": "Disney / Freelance (Creator of Goofy, Mushroom Dance in Fantasia)",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 1",
              "content": "If you can't draw - forget it. You're an actor without arms and legs."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 2",
              "content": "The knowledge that went into making little drawings come to life is in the early Disneys... The mechanics of the old Disney animation remain."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 3",
              "content": "Invent! Every rule in animation is there to be broken - if you have the inventiveness and curiosity to look beyond what exists."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_04",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 4",
              "content": "A good dancer invents. It's not natural for a person to leap into the air - do scissors with their feet and then land on their toes. We can do anything we want as long as we make it 'work' - make it look believable."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_05",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 5",
              "content": "That's too realistic - one of the things about animation is that it's not like life! (On animating on ones vs. twos)"
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "mentor_04",
          "title": "Grim Natwick",
          "studio_affiliation": "Fleischer / Disney (Creator of Betty Boop, lead animator on Snow White)",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 1",
              "content": "A-a-animation... it's.. a-a-all... in the timing.... a-a-and in... the spacing... (long pause)... stray-y-y-n-nge.... that the Americans.... were the ones to work this out..."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 2",
              "content": "Bad inbetweens will kill the finest animation."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_03",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 3",
              "content": "We used to bet ten dollars against ten cents that you could take any character and walk it across the room and get a laugh out of it."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_04",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 4",
              "content": "Curves are beautiful to watch. (On circling key drawings)"
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "mentor_05",
          "title": "Bill Tytla",
          "studio_affiliation": "Disney (Animator of Stromboli in Pinocchio, Chernabog in Fantasia, Dumbo)",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 1",
              "content": "At times you will have to animate stuff where you can't just be cute and coy. Those are the times when you'll have to know something about drawing. Whether it's called form or force or vitality, you must get it into your work, for that will be what you feel, and drawing is your means of expressing it."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 2",
              "content": "If you do a piece of animation and run over it enough times, you must see what's wrong with it."
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "chapter_id": "mentor_06",
          "title": "Tex Avery",
          "studio_affiliation": "Warner Bros. / MGM (Master of wild cartoon slapstick, Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Droopy)",
          "sections": [
            {
              "section_id": "section_01",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 1",
              "content": "In the 40s Director Tex Avery pushed the limits - inventively defying gravity - going faster and faster for his split second gags."
            },
            {
              "section_id": "section_02",
              "title": "Teaching / Quote 2",
              "content": "Tex went in the opposite direction, celebrating the cartoon as cartoon, exploring the medium's potential for surrealism."
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
